title: Florida JEAC Opinion 2026-03
subject: A judge may not execute an affidavit prepared by counsel regarding the circumstances surrounding the judge’s submission of a letter of retirement, but the judge may appear at a deposition concerning the same subject, keeping in mind the ethical constraints when providing testimony in a pending proceeding
text:
ISSUE
1. May a judge execute an affidavit prepared by counsel regarding the circumstances surrounding the judge’s submission of a letter of retirement?
ANSWER: No.
2. May the judge appear at a deposition concerning the same subject?
ANSWER: Yes, keeping in mind the ethical constraints when providing testimony in a pending proceeding.

FACTS
The inquiring judge recently submitted a letter of retirement, [1] which was addressed to the Chief Justice of the Florida Supreme Court with a copy sent to the Chief Judge of the inquiring judge’s circuit. In the letter, the judge stated an intention to retire effective December 31, 2026. The letter was forwarded to the Governor’s office.
A legal dispute has now arisen concerning the judge’s anticipated retirement from the bench. An election for the inquiring judge’s position was scheduled, but then subsequently canceled when the Governor’s office announced its intention to fill the judge’s seat by appointment. The cancellation of the election is currently the subject of a pending declaratory judgment action.
On May 17, 2026, counsel for the plaintiffs in the declaratory judgment action transmitted correspondence to the circuit court’s public information officer in which counsel requested the inquiring judge to provide “a brief, narrowly tailored affidavit” confirming certain alleged factual matters surrounding the judge’s retirement letter. The correspondence listed five particular topics that counsel would like to have addressed in the affidavit. The affidavit was requested, in part, to dispense with the necessity of taking the inquiring judge’s deposition (presumably on the same topics of inquiry).
The inquiring judge asks whether the judge can provide this affidavit in light of Canon 2(B) of the Florida Code of Judicial Conduct. And if not, the judge wishes to know whether the judge can appear for a deposition and testify concerning the submission of the retirement letter.
[1] We refer to this correspondence as a “letter of retirement” or a “retirement letter” because that is how the inquiring judge referred to it in the inquiry. This Committee has no power or authority to construe the legal effect of this document. Nor can this Committee engage in any kind of fact-finding. As with all inquiries, we accept the facts that an inquiring judge chooses to present to us as if they are accurate and complete. The advice we provide in this opinion, like in all our opinions, is subject to the caveat of that assumption.

DISCUSSION
The concern identified by the inquiring judge in the underlying inquiry—the applicability of Canon 2B—is warranted. Canon 2B states:
A judge shall not allow family, social, political or other relationships to influence the judge's judicial conduct or judgment. A judge shall not lend the prestige of judicial office to advance the private interests of the judge or others; nor shall a judge convey or permit others to convey the impression that they are in a special position to influence the judge. A judge shall not testify voluntarily as a character witness.
Although the most intuitively applicable part of this canon only prohibits voluntary testimony as a “character witness,” this Committee has issued numerous opinions warning judges not to voluntarily provide testimony on factual matters as well, unless compelled to do so under a subpoena, or unless the matter concerns official investigations by a law enforcement agency, the Bar, or the Judicial Qualifications Commission. See, e.g., Fla. JEAC Op. 03-04 (observing that “Canon 2B does not state that a judge cannot voluntarily testify as to factual issues; rather, it limits the proscribed conduct to voluntarily testifying as a ‘character’ witness. However, Canon 2B also prohibits a judge from lending the prestige of judicial office to advance the private interests of the judge or others. Therefore, a judge voluntarily testifying as to factual issues is lending the prestige of his or her office to one side or the other in a disputed matter, and for that reason, the judge should not voluntarily testify as to factual matters”); Fla. JEAC Op. 21-13 (determining that a judge could provide a sworn statement to the Office of Inspector General concerning a police officer’s conduct in the judge’s courtroom); see also Fla. JEAC Op. 97-01 (summarizing prior opinions and stating, “the Committee on Standards of Conduct Governing Judges has generally taken the position that where the testimony of a sitting judge is permissible, the judge should only testify pursuant to a subpoena”).
The inquiring judge should be especially reticent under the circumstances described in the inquiry. First, the affidavit is being sought in connection with a private, civil dispute, not a criminal investigation or a Bar or a JQC investigation. Second, the affidavit is sought at the behest of an attorney representing one side in that dispute. Voluntarily drafting and then submitting such an affidavit under these circumstances could be perceived as assisting the plaintiffs in a pending lawsuit, and, thus, could create the impression that the judge was lending the prestige of judicial office to favor that side. That kind of appearance of impropriety is what Canon 2, generally, and Canon 2B, specifically, seek to prevent.
As to the second inquiry, the judge appearing at a deposition pursuant to a subpoena, we have little guidance to offer given the information we have been presented. Cf. Fla. JEAC Op. 24-09 (opining in an inquiry with “unique and specific” facts concerning a judge providing testimony in a civil lawsuit involving divorced parents, a therapist, and a previous perjury prosecution, that “[w]hile the Committee can opine multiple reasons why this testimony would not be otherwise admissible in any proceeding, we find that there are no Canons that are implicated in such testimony”). The limitations of deposing judicial officers more often present legal questions than ethical ones. Cf. Fla. Bar. v. Girley , 417 So. 3d 230, 237 (Fla. 2025) (“Accordingly, we have recognized the general rule that 'judges cannot be compelled to testify as to matters concerning their judicial duties,' and we have held that inquiring into a 'judge's thought process' is impermissible.” (quoting State v. Lewis , 656 So. 2d 1248, 1250 (Fla. 1994))). However, a judge is constrained by the Code of Judicial Conduct at all times, including when he or she gives testimony in a deposition. Thus, the inquiring judge should remain mindful of all the judicial canons, including Canon 3B(12) (“A judge shall not disclose or use, for any purpose unrelated to judicial duties, nonpublic information acquired in a judicial capacity.”).

REFERENCES
Fla. Bar. v. Girley , 417 So. 3d 230 (Fla. 2025)
State v. Lewis , 656 So. 2d 1248 (Fla. 1994)
Fla. Code Jud. Conduct, Canons 2B, 3B
Fla. JEAC Ops. 1997-01, 2003-04, 2021-13, 2024-09

SUBJECT
A judge may not execute an affidavit prepared by counsel regarding the circumstances surrounding the judge’s submission of a letter of retirement, but the judge may appear at a deposition concerning the same subject, keeping in mind the ethical constraints when providing testimony in a pending proceeding
